description: Drop Morgan bit columns that are set in fewer than 5% or more than 95% of the training molecules (mask computed on training features only and applied to the test features), leaving the random forest settings unchanged.

issues: No sign of getting around the measurement. There is no file or network access and no pasted answers. Test labels are never used: the scaffold groups come only from train_smiles, and the early-stopping validation split is drawn only from the training rows (Xa).

No bug that makes the result meaningless. The diff changes the method in two ways. First, LightGBM now stops early on a 10% split grouped by Murcko scaffold and is then refit on all rows for 1.1 times the best iteration count. Second, the out-of-fold stacking with a positive Ridge meta-model is removed, and the three base predictions are now averaged with equal weights.
My guess at why the loss got worse: dropping the learned stacking weights probably accounts for most of it, since a plain mean gives equal weight to a weaker base learner.

Recomputed z: the difference is 0.5826 − 0.5357 = 0.0469. The standard error is 0.0042 × √(1/1 + 1/1) ≈ 0.00594, so z ≈ −7.90, which matches the harness's −7.904. The candidate is much worse, so reject is correct.
Only one run each for the candidate and the incumbent, but a 0.047 gap is far beyond the noise, so the conclusion holds.

Effectiveness concern, not a bug: the BRICS hashed counts go through the same 1st-99th percentile clipping as the descriptors. Most of the 512 sparse bins are nonzero in fewer than 1% of molecules, so their 99th percentile is 0. Clipping then sets those columns to 0 and throws away most of the BRICS signal. Consider excluding the BRICS block from clipping.

Speed and cosmetics: BRICS decomposition is not cached, so it runs again on every one of the 15 fits. That is probably fine within 10 minutes for 3360 molecules, but caching it like desc_vector would be cleaner. The comment in brics_counts repeats the docstring note of _frag_hash. BRICSDecompose would crash on an unparseable SMILES (MolFromSmiles returns None), but the benchmark SMILES should all parse, as the existing descriptor code already assumes.

The crash is a width mismatch: base_predict returns four base-learner columns (RF, LightGBM, KRR, ElasticNet) but the out-of-fold array was allocated with three, so I changed the allocation to four columns.

issues: No sign of getting around the measurement. The diff only changes LightGBM hyperparameters: it switches to DART boosting (drop_rate=0.1, skip_drop=0.5, max_drop=50) and lowers N_ROUNDS from 600 to 400. It adds no file access, no pasted answers and no use of test labels.

No bug that would make the result meaningless. One caveat: LightGBM's DART does not work properly with early stopping or best_iteration. If the unchanged code around this diff uses early stopping or a validation split to pick the number of rounds, the DART runs would be using the wrong round count. That would make the comparison less fair, but it would not make the result invalid.

The numbers support the reject. The candidate scores 0.4914 against the incumbent's 0.4895, which is 0.0019 worse. Recomputing with noise sd 0.0042 and one run each gives z = (0.4895 - 0.4914) / (0.0042 * sqrt(2)) ≈ -0.32. The harness's -0.315 differs only by rounding of the 4-decimal values.
The candidate is only 0.3 sd worse, so this is not evidence that DART is worse. It is just no evidence of improvement. DART also costs more compute per round.

Smooth the stack's test predictions with 20 steps of label propagation over a kNN (k=10) Tanimoto graph built on the union of training and test ECFP bits, clamping training rows to their true labels.

Add a second kernel-ridge stack member using the product kernel K = Tanimoto(ECFP) * RBF(standardised descriptors), with its lambda chosen from the same grid by the existing inner grouped CV, and feed it to the meta-learner as a fourth column alongside the unchanged sum-kernel member.

Train the LightGBM base learner in two stages: 400 rounds of Huber (delta = median absolute deviation of the training targets), then 300 more rounds continued from that model with regression_l1 at learning rate 0.01, keeping leaves 31, min_child_samples 10 and feature_fraction 0.2.

The crash happens because the LightGBM Dataset is built with default free_raw_data=True, so it is freed after the first lgb.train and cannot be reused when continuing training with init_model; setting free_raw_data=False on that Dataset fixes it.

issues: No sign of gaming the measurement. wl_counts only reads the SMILES strings and RDKit graph structure. It never touches labels, files or the network. Featurizing test_smiles without labels works the same way as the existing featurize and descriptor code.

The descriptor slice is updated correctly. Before, Xa[:, 2*N_BITS:] would have picked up the new WL columns. Now it is limited to 2*N_BITS : 2*N_BITS+N_DESC, so the descriptor ridge/linear block still sees only the clipped descriptors. This assumes the descriptor block has exactly len(Descriptors._descList) columns, which it does if the incumbent computes every descriptor in _descList. The Tanimoto kernel still uses only the first N_BITS columns.
The _crc hash is deterministic and does not depend on Python's hash seed. Inputs and outputs do not depend on the seed, so results are reproducible.

Runtime risk: _crc is a pure-Python loop over bytes. It runs roughly 2 times per atom per iteration across 4 iterations, for every train and test molecule in every fit. That could add tens of seconds or more across the 15 fits. Check this against the 10-minute limit if the incumbent is already slow. If needed, compute WL counts once per SMILES and cache them, or use a cheaper hash.
Minor: WL counts go in raw, not clipped or scaled. That is fine for trees, and the linear block excludes them.
No harness numbers are available yet (no run), so there are no claims to check and z cannot be recomputed.

description: Append a hashed 1024-bucket Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree count block (iterations 0 to 3, zlib.crc32 bucketing) after the descriptors, and bound the RBF descriptor slice so the kernel still uses only the RDKit descriptor columns.

The job timed out because each of the 15 fits runs six base_predict calls (five OOF folds plus the full fit), and each call grows a 200-tree random forest on about 3,260 features and runs a 9-config nested kernel grid search; I cut the forest to 100 trees with max_features=0.1 and trimmed the kernel grid from 9 to 4 configurations, which should bring each fit well under the 40 s budget (estimate, not timed).
Replace the kernel ridge member's final squared-error solve with a 15-step IRLS absolute-error solve (per-sample ridge lam*max(|residual|,0.05)) using the grid-searched lambda and RBF weight.

issues: No sign of getting around the measurement. There is no file or network access and no pasted answers. The test labels are never used: KRR and IRLS are fit only on ya, Fa and Za, and the test features only enter through Kb.

The IRLS update looks correct for a weighted kernel ridge with L1-like weights. Minimising sum_i w_i r_i^2 + lam*a'Ka gives (K + lam*W^-1)a = y - mu, with W^-1 = diag(max(|r|, 0.05)). That is what the code does.

The diff mixes three changes: RF trees drop from 200 to 100, the (lam, wr) grid shrinks to a single point, and IRLS replaces the plain KRR solve. A z near zero can't tell which change helps or hurts. The 200-to-100 tree cut alone could cost some accuracy.

With one config left, the inner GroupKFold loop is dead code: it fits 4 folds and can only pick (0.5, 1.0). It also scores plain ridge rather than the IRLS model that is actually used. It should be removed or made to score IRLS.

z check: (0.4895 - 0.4912) / (0.0042 * sqrt(1/1 + 1/1)) ≈ -0.286. This matches the harness's -0.281 within the rounding of the 4-decimal values. The candidate is slightly worse and well inside the noise, so rejecting it is justified.

Shrink the stacked prediction toward the training mean by a similarity-based weight, w = clip((s - a)/(b - a), 0, 1), where s is each molecule's max ECFP Tanimoto similarity to the training set, with (a, b) chosen from a 5x5 grid by lowest MAE on leave-one-out-similarity OOF stack predictions.

The job exceeded 600 s because the kernel ridge branch ran a 9-config inner grid search (36 dense solves of about 2700x2700 per base_predict, across 6 base_predict calls per fit), so I fixed the KRR hyperparameters and halved the random forest's trees to cut the per-fit cost.

Augment the random forest and LightGBM members with two bit-dropout copies of the fingerprint block (10% of bits zeroed per copy) and average their predictions over the clean test matrix plus three seeded dropout copies; the kernel member is unchanged.

The job exceeded 600 s because each fit runs base_predict six times, and each call fits a 200-tree random forest and LightGBM on 3x-augmented data, then predicts with 4x test-time augmentation. I cut the augmentation copies and TTA passes and halve the forest size, which removes most of the runtime while keeping the same three-learner stack.

Replace the positive Ridge meta-learner with an L1 (MAE) convex stacker solved by linprog (HiGHS): non-negative weights summing to 1 plus an intercept bounded by the range of y, with the simple average as fallback.

The job timed out because each fit_predict runs about 90 kernel-ridge solves in a 3x3 hyperparameter grid with 4-fold inner CV, plus 200-tree random forests; I cut the KRR grid to the single default setting and halve the forest size to fit within 600 s.

After the stacked meta prediction, add 0.5 times a similarity-weighted mean of the OOF residuals of up to 10 training neighbours with ECFP Tanimoto similarity above 0.4 (zero correction when none pass).

The job timed out because each fit_predict runs base_predict six times, and each call does a 200-tree random forest on about 2260 features plus a 9-config by 4-fold kernel ridge grid search; I cut the RF to 100 trees with max_features 0.1 and fix the kernel ridge hyperparameters so the grid search is skipped.

The job timed out because each fit_predict runs base_predict about 6 times (5 OOF folds plus the final fit), and each call does a 9-point kernel-ridge hyperparameter grid (36 linear solves on about 2150x2150 matrices) plus a 200-tree random forest on about 2250 features, so 15 fits exceed 600 s. The fix collapses the KRR grid to the single setting (lam=0.5, wr=1.0) and halves the random forest to 100 trees.

Replace the RBF kernel on the z-scored descriptor block with a Laplacian kernel exp(-gamma * L1 distance), with gamma = 1/(n_descriptors * mean training-fold L1 distance) computed via scipy cdist, leaving the Tanimoto term and the lambda/weight grid unchanged.

The job timed out because each fit_predict call runs 6 base_predict calls, and each of those runs a 9-configuration kernel grid search (9 x 4 dense 1650-sized solves) plus a 200-tree random forest; I cut the kernel grid to the single setting (lam=0.5, wr=1.0) and halve the forest size to fit within 600 s.

Adds one pH 7.4 log10 neutral-fraction feature, computed from a small SMARTS table of ionisable groups and capped at -4, as an extra column for the RF and LightGBM inputs only, with the kernel members' descriptor slice excluded so they stay unchanged.

The job timed out because base_predict runs a 9-point kernel hyperparameter grid with 4 inner folds (36 dense 2000x2000 solves) on each of the 90 calls; I fix the kernel settings to one config and halve the random forest size to keep all 15 fits under 600 s.

Add a pairwise-difference LightGBM base learner (20000 random training pairs, ECFP-bit plus standardised-descriptor differences, L1 loss on y_i minus y_j, median over 100 anchors) as a fourth stack member.

Trim the 5% of training rows with the largest absolute OOF meta residuals, then refit the meta Ridge and the base learners on the kept rows (reusing the existing OOF predictions, so the job still makes only six base_predict calls).

The 600 s timeout came mainly from the nested grid search over the kernel ridge (lam, wr) settings: 9 configs x 4 inner folds of ~2000x2000 dense solves, repeated in every base_predict call (6 per fit, 15 fits). I fix the kernel settings at lam=0.5, wr=1.0 and cut the random forest from 200 to 100 trees.
Weight each training molecule by 1/sqrt(number of training molecules sharing its Murcko scaffold) and pass these as sample_weight to the random forest fit inside base_predict.

The job timed out because base_predict's kernel-ridge hyperparameter grid (9 configs x 4 inner folds of ~2000-sample solves, repeated in every one of the 90 base_predict calls) dominates runtime; I fix the KRR settings to the single default (lam=0.5, wr=1.0) and halve the random forest size to bring the 15-fit job well under 600 s.

Map the training targets to Gaussian normal scores (rank, then (r-0.5)/n, then norm.ppf) before all base learners and the meta Ridge, and back-map the final predictions through the training-target quantiles at norm.cdf(score), clipped to the observed range.

The job timed out because the kernel-ridge hyperparameter grid search re-solves 36 dense ~2000x2000 systems inside every base_predict call (about 90 calls in total), so I fixed lam and wr at the best-typical values and cut the random forest to 100 trees with max_features 0.1 to save time; this is untested, so expect to check the timing.

The job timed out because each fit ran a nested stacking scheme (5 inner folds plus a full refit, each with an RF, LightGBM, and a 36-solve KRR grid search), so I removed the inner CV, the KRR grid search, and the meta-learner, and average the three base learners at fixed KRR settings.

The job exceeded the 600 s limit mainly because base_predict runs a 9-config inner grid search (36 dense 2000x2000 solves) on every outer fold and on the final fit, across 15 fits; I collapse that grid to the single lam=0.5, wr=1.0 setting and halve the random forest to 100 trees to cut runtime.

Add a fourth stack member, a kernel ridge (lam=0.5, no grid) on the Tanimoto similarity of unit-normalised ErG reduced-graph fingerprints, computed in fit_predict and passed into base_predict, with the meta-learner widened to four columns.

The job timed out because each fit_predict runs six base_predict calls (five OOF folds plus the final fit), and each call grid-searches 9 KRR settings with 4-fold inner solves on roughly 2,700×2,700 matrices. Add a fourth stack member: a min_samples_leaf=5 random forest whose leaf-sharing proximity kernel (sparse one-hot leaves, averaged over trees) feeds a fixed-lambda (0.5) kernel ridge, with its prediction appended to the stacked base columns and the OOF width raised to 4.

The job timed out because each fit_predict ran base_predict six times (five nested out-of-fold passes plus the final pass), and each call fits two 200-tree random forests, LightGBM, and a kernel grid search. Add a fourth base learner to base_predict: kernel ridge (lam=0.5, no grid) on exp(-L1/s) over Morgan ECFP count vectors, with s the median training L1 distance, computed via a threshold-indicator matmul trick so no 3D broadcast is needed.

The job exceeded the 600 s limit because the 15 fits each run base_predict six times, and each call fits a 200-tree random forest on about 2200 features, 600 LightGBM rounds, and a count-based L1 kernel built with float64 matmuls; this cuts the forest size and feature sampling, halves the LightGBM rounds, and runs the L1 kernel in float32 (exact for these integer counts).

Replace the kernel-ridge member with an average of 8 fixed-hyperparameter kernel ridge fits, each on a random 50% subset of the ECFP bit columns (seeded by seed + j), using scipy's positive-definite solver for speed.

issues: No sign of getting around the measurement. The diff adds no file or network access and no hard-coded answers, and it does not use test labels. test_smiles are only featurized and predicted, as before.

No bug that would make the result meaningless. A plain average of the three base learners replaces the fitted Ridge meta-learner. Its randomness comes from the seed argument (seed + j). These changes make the model weaker but leave the evaluation valid.

Minor robustness point: on a random half of the bits, a sparse molecule could share no set bits with another, making the Tanimoto denominator 0. That would give NaN unless tanimoto() handles it. The run finished with a finite loss, so it did not affect this result.
Minor: lam and wr are still chosen with the full-bit kernel, then reused for the half-bit kernels, so they may not suit those kernels. This is a design weakness, not an integrity problem.

The numbers are consistent. The candidate scored 0.5176 against the incumbent's 0.4895, which is 0.0281 worse. With one run each and noise sd 0.0042, the sd of the difference is 0.0042*sqrt(2) ≈ 0.00594, so z ≈ -4.73. The harness gave -4.744; the small gap is probably rounding in the adjusted values. Rejecting is correct.

description: The job timed out because each fit_predict ran base_predict six times (five out-of-fold passes for stacking plus one full pass), and each pass fits a 200-tree random forest, a 600-round LightGBM model, and a kernel grid search with eight kernel solves. I replace the stacking step with a plain average of the three base learners, so base_predict runs once per fit, and I cut the forest to 100 trees for extra headroom.
